{"id": "fb36dd06-7023-44e5-9798-0d22903ed455", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_cJLzQ4Z8iC5kzHt5b2x00S", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Create lifecycle rule\",\"context\":\"# Create lifecycle rule\\n\\nAn Amazon S3 Lifecycle rule configures predefined actions to perform on objects during\\ntheir lifetime. You can create a lifecycle rule to optimize your objects' storage\\ncosts throughout their lifetime.\\n\\nYou can define the scope of the lifecycle rule to all objects in your bucket or to\\nobjects\\nwith a shared prefix, certain object tags, or a certain object size.\\n\\nYou can specify one or more predefined actions for Amazon S3 to perform. There are\\ntwo types of\\nactions: *transition* and *expiration*. Transition actions define when objects transition to a storage\\nclass for less-frequently accessed objects. Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. For\\nmore\\ninformation about which storage classes you can transition objects to and the constraints\\nof\\nobject size, minimum days, and cost considerations, see Supported transitions and related constraints.\\n\\nWhen you create a new S3 Lifecycle rule Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to your\\nLifecycle configuration that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned.\\nYou can allow smaller objects to transition by adding an **Object size** filter that specifies a smaller size to each applicable rule. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. To do this, use the\\noptional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. For details on\\npricing,\\nsee **Lifecycle Transition requests** pricing on the **Requests\\n& data retrievals** tab and **Storage pricing** on the\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-create-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Lifecycle rule details\",\"context\":\"# Lifecycle rule details\\n\\nYou can configure Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to store your objects cost-effectively\\nthroughout their lifetime. You can instruct Amazon S3 to transition objects to less-expensive\\nstorage classes or to archive or delete objects.\\n\\nUse this page to see the scope of the selected S3 Lifecycle rule. You can also view\\ntransition and expiration actions for current and noncurrent object versions, based\\non your\\nlifecycle rule.\\n\\nFor **Current version actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be transitioned and *the storage\\n class* to transition that version to.\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be expired.\\n\\nFor **Noncurrent versions actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* after which a noncurrent version will be transitioned and\\n *the storage class* to transition that version\\n to.\\n* After the transition, *the number of newest noncurrent\\n versions* to retain.\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* to permanent deletion and *the number of\\n newest noncurrent versions* to retain afterward.\\n\\nUnder **Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart\\nuploads**, there are two sections of configuration information:\\n\\n* You can see if your lifecycle rule is configured to delete expired object delete\\n markers. An expired object delete marker occurs when all object versions are\\n deleted, and only a single delete marker remains. If you selected this option in\\n your lifecycle rule, an expired object delete marker will be deleted.\\n* You can also see if your lifecycle rule deletes incomplete multipart uploads after\\n a specified number of days\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-view-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Cost optimization in analytics services\",\"context\":\"##### Amazon S3 lifecycle policies\\n\\nA\\nlifecycle\\npolicy automatically move objects in your bucket from\\none storage class to another. Regular data cleanup into\\ndistinct storage classes is crucial in the big data\\nprocessing. Data lakes have different data layers like\\nsource, raw, process, and business data. Once the data is\\nprocessed, the source and raw data layers are rarely\\naccessed. As a result, transitioning them to infrequent and\\narchive storage class could save money. You can avoid the\\nmanual cleanup process with lifecycle policies to save on\\ncosts.\\n\\nCreate a lifecycle rule to automatically transition your\\nobjects to Standard-IA storage class, archive them to\\nGlacier storage class, and remove them after a specified\\nperiod.\\n\\nLifecycle transition costs are directly proportional to the\\nnumber of objects transitioned, so reduce the number of\\nobjects by aggregating or zipping and compressing them\\nbefore moving them to archive tiers. Apply life cycle\\npolicies to the source, staging, and other data sets that\\nare processed and would no longer be needed.\\n\\nCreate lifecycle policies to clean up incomplete multipart\\nuploads. Also, you can organize data to make life cycle\\npolicies simpler and more effective. For example, keep all\\nsource data under one prefix so you can have a single\\nlifecycle policy for all the source data sets rather than\\none for each source prefix. In addition, use lifecycle\\npolicies to delete many objects to avoid S3 API costs.\\nFinally, if your bucket is versioned, ensure there is a rule\\naction for both current and non-current objects to either\\ntransition or expire\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/cost-modeling-data-lakes/cost-optimization-in-analytics-services.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check S3 lifecycle cost optimization documentation"}

{"id": "c57a46fa-a362-4b7b-8a62-6a7740360799", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "S3 Lifecycle rules save money in a few ways. Here is how to use them.

## What lifecycle rules can do

- **Transition actions** move objects to cheaper storage classes as they age. Examples are Standard → Standard-IA or Intelligent-Tiering → Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive.
- **Expiration actions** permanently delete objects you no longer need.

Both kinds of action run asynchronously. Your bill is updated as if they happened immediately.

## Where the biggest savings usually are

1. **Tier down data that cools off.** Logs, backups, raw or staging data and old exports are rarely read after the first 30 to 90 days. Move them to an infrequent-access or archive class, then expire them when your retention period ends.
2. **Clean up old versions in versioned buckets.** Noncurrent versions keep costing money until a rule removes them. Add actions for noncurrent versions: transition or expire them after N days, and optionally keep the newest N versions. Also enable removal of expired object delete markers.
3. **Abort incomplete multipart uploads.** Failed uploads leave hidden parts that you pay for. A rule such as "abort after 7 days" costs nothing and is one of the easiest wins.
4. **Expire data you don't need.** For temporary or processed-and-discarded data, use a plain expiration rule. Deleting objects in bulk with a rule also avoids per-request API costs.

## Pitfalls to watch for

- **Small objects:** by default, objects under 128 KB are not transitioned. Transitions cost per request, so moving millions of tiny objects can cost more than it saves. Consider aggregating or compressing them first. You can override the 128 KB default with an object-size filter on the rule.
- **Transition request charges:** every transition has a per-object fee. Cost scales with object count, not size.
- **Minimum storage durations and retrieval fees:** IA and archive classes have minimum storage durations and retrieval charges. Don't move data you still read often. For unpredictable access patterns, **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** avoids that risk.
- **Deletes are permanent:** consider versioning, Object Lock, MFA delete or replication as safeguards before adding expiration rules.
- **Organize by prefix or tag:** keeping similar data under one prefix, such as all raw data under `raw/`, lets one rule cover it. You can also scope rules by tags or object size.

## A sensible starter policy

| Rule | Scope | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Abort incomplete multipart uploads | Whole bucket | After 7 days |
| Logs / backups | `logs/` prefix | → Standard-IA at 30 days, → Glacier at 90 days, expire at 365 days (adjust to your retention) |
| Noncurrent versions | Whole bucket, if versioned | Transition or expire after 30 days, keep the newest 3 |
| Expired delete markers | Whole bucket, if versioned | Remove |

To base the rules on your actual data, I can review your S3 buckets in this account. I'd look at which buckets are largest, whether versioning is on, which ones have no lifecycle configuration, and how many incomplete multipart uploads they hold. Tell me if you want that, or give me a specific bucket to start with.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
